title: Instance-Level Costs for Nuanced Classifier Evaluation
claim: Cost-weighted error is consistently lower than standard error rate across tasks and model types, showing most mistakes are low-cost.
layout: 2 side-by-side grouped bar charts, left-to-right, paired NEC vs error bars
description: Two grouped bar charts side by side. Panel (a), labeled 'Frozen embeddings / linear classifiers', shows six tasks on the x-axis: Jigsaw (TF-IDF), Jigsaw (RoBERTa), Turkey, NHANES, iNaturalist and Synthetic. Panel (b), labeled 'Fine-tuned models', is larger and shows three tasks: Jigsaw (RoBERTa), Turkey (ResNet) and iNaturalist (ResNet). Each task has a blue NEC bar next to an orange error-rate bar, with black error bars. The y-axis is Metric (%). The orange bar is taller than the blue bar in every group. The gap is largest for Jigsaw and NHANES, and smaller for iNaturalist. Each panel has a legend in its top corner. The eye goes first to the tall orange and blue bars for NHANES in (a) and iNaturalist in (b). Panel (a) has empty space above it.
caption: NEC vs Error Rate across datasets. Blue bars show NEC (cost-weighted error); orange bars show standard error rate. Fine-tuning improves both metrics while preserving the NEC/error-rate gap.
abstract: Standard classification treats all errors equally, but in applications such as content moderation and medical screening, mistakes on clear-cut cases are more costly than errors on ambiguous ones. From a contextual bandit framework, we propose normalized excess cost (NEC), a metric that weighs classification errors by per-example costs and reduces to standard error rate when costs are uniform. Costs can derive from annotator vote margins, distance from decision thresholds, or confidence ratings. Across text, image, and tabular benchmarks, we find that NEC is often substantially lower than error rate: models with 5% error rate can achieve 1.8% NEC, revealing that most mistakes concentrate on ambiguous, low-cost examples. We also find that incorporating costs into training via loss weighting, sampling strategies, or regression yields inconsistent benefits. Our framework provides a practical methodology for deriving and evaluating instance-level misclassification costs, even if cost-sensitive training offers limited benefit.
